\chapter{Two Things Joined}
\label{ch:sa-two-things-joined}
\hlchaptermodality{52}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two Sanskrit nouns with and, offer a choice between them with or, set one clause against another with but, and deny both with a doubled na.}

Complete SA-R52-joins and say all four joins in order, naming for each one where it stands in the sentence.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ca]{\sk{च} (ca) — and}

\label{lesson:SA-C52-ca}



\begin{quote}
Two words back: what does \emph{mātāmahī} mean, and who is a \emph{mātulaḥ}? You can now name a great many things one at a time. You cannot yet name two.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{च}}
\textbf{\sk{च}} (\emph{ca}) — \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}.

One syllable, and until this lesson the track had no way to put two things in one sentence. Everything you have learnt to name — a house, a river, a mother, a moon — you have named alone.

\textbf{\sk{च} does not stand between the two things. It stands after the second one.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{अन्नं} \sk{पानीयं} \sk{च}} — \emph{annaṁ pānīyaṁ ca} — \textbf{food and water}
\end{quote}

English puts \emph{and} in the gap. Sanskrit puts \textbf{\sk{च}} at the end and leaves the gap empty. Read the phrase again and notice that nothing sits between the two nouns at all: they are simply placed side by side, and \textbf{\sk{च}} at the back is what tells you they were a pair.

\textbf{\sk{च}} can never begin a sentence. A word that must lean on the word before it is called an \textbf{enclitic}, and this is Sanskrit's commonest one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two things in one sentence, for the first time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mātulaḥ}, then read \textbf{\sk{मातामही}} and say what it means
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{annaṁ pānīyaṁ ca}, said once slowly and once at speed
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{annaṁ pānīyaṁ ca}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{च}}, and say where in the phrase it stands
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{च}} mean, and where does it stand? (\textquotedblleft{}And\textquotedblright{}, and after the second thing.) Say \textquotedblleft{}food and water\textquotedblright{} once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vā]{\sk{वा} (vā) — or}

\label{lesson:SA-C52-va}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}food and water\textquotedblright{}, and then say where \textbf{\sk{च}} stood in it. Then say \emph{mātulaḥ}, from two chapters back, and who it names.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वा}}
\textbf{\sk{वा}} (\emph{vā}) — \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.

Everything you have just learnt about \textbf{\sk{च}} is true of \textbf{\sk{वा}}, unchanged. It is an enclitic; it goes after the second item; it cannot open a sentence.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{पानीयं} \sk{क्षीरं} \sk{वा}} — \emph{pānīyaṁ kṣīraṁ vā} — \textbf{water or milk}
\end{quote}

So the two words share one slot, and swapping them swaps the meaning of the whole phrase without moving anything else:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{पानीयं} \sk{क्षीरं} \sk{च}} — water \textbf{and} milk
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{पानीयं} \sk{क्षीरं} \sk{वा}} — water \textbf{or} milk
\end{quote}

That is worth pausing on. In English \emph{and} and \emph{or} are two different words in the same middle position. In Sanskrit they are two different words in the same \textbf{final} position, and the sentence around them does not shift at all.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Both halves of the joining pair: \textbf{\sk{च}} for both, \textbf{\sk{वा}} for either.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pānīyaṁ kṣīraṁ vā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same two nouns with \textbf{\sk{च}} instead, and say what changed
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{पानीयं} \sk{क्षीरं} \sk{वा}}, then say what it means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\sk{च}} and \textbf{\sk{वा}} means \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}? Say \textquotedblleft{}water or milk\textquotedblright{}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kintu]{\sk{किन्तु} (kintu) — but}

\label{lesson:SA-C52-kintu}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}water or milk\textquotedblright{}. Then say what \textbf{\sk{किम्}} means on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{किन्तु}}
\textbf{\sk{किन्तु}} (\emph{kintu}) — \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.

Look at it before you use it. It is \textbf{\sk{किम्}} — the question word you have held since your first questions — welded to the small particle \textbf{\sk{तु}}, \textquotedblleft{}however\textquotedblright{}. \emph{What-however}. Sanskrit built its \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{} out of a question and a shrug.

And here is the thing that matters for using it: \textbf{\sk{किन्तु} is not an enclitic.} Unlike \textbf{\sk{च}} and \textbf{\sk{वा}} it does not lean backwards. It stands at the \textbf{front} of the clause it contradicts.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{बालः} \sk{गच्छति} \sk{किन्तु} \sk{गुरुः} \sk{न} \sk{गच्छति}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bālaḥ gacchati kintu guruḥ na gacchati}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{the boy goes, but the teacher does not go}
\end{quote}

Three joining words, two different habits. Say the rule to yourself once: \textbf{\sk{च}} and \textbf{\sk{वा}} go last, \textbf{\sk{किन्तु}} goes first.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three joins: add, offer, contradict.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ gacchati kintu guruḥ na gacchati}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{किन्तु}}, and find the \textbf{\sk{किम्}} inside it
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\sk{वा}} at the end of its phrase, \textbf{\sk{किन्तु}} at the front of its clause
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\sk{किन्तु}} mean, and where does it stand? (\textquotedblleft{}But\textquotedblright{}, and first.) Say the boy-and-teacher sentence once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na … na]{\sk{न} … \sk{न} (na … na) — neither … nor}

\label{lesson:SA-C52-na-na}



\begin{quote}
Where does \textbf{\sk{किन्तु}} stand in its clause? And what does \textbf{\sk{न}} mean on its own?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the fourth join needs no new word}]
You have had \textbf{\sk{न}} since the very first chapter. Said once it denies one thing. \textbf{Said twice, once before each item, it denies both.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\sk{न} \sk{अन्नं} \sk{न} \sk{पानीयम्}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{na annaṁ na pānīyam}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{neither food nor water}
\end{quote}

There is no new vocabulary here at all. The join is made out of repetition, which is why Sanskrit never needed a word like English \emph{neither}.

Set the four joins of this chapter side by side and the pattern in their positions is the whole lesson:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{join} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{where it stands} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\sk{च}} & and & after the second item \\
\textbf{\sk{वा}} & or & after the second item \\
\textbf{\sk{किन्तु}} & but & first in its clause \\
\textbf{\sk{न} … \sk{न}} & neither … nor & before each item \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three positions, four joins. Nothing else about the sentence moves.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every basic join: both, either, contrary, and neither.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{na annaṁ na pānīyam}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bālaḥ na khādati} — the boy does not eat — then double the \textbf{\sk{न}} to deny both nouns
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\sk{न} \sk{अन्नं} \sk{न} \sk{पानीयम्}}, then say what it means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Sanskrit say \textquotedblleft{}neither … nor\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\sk{न}} before each item.) Say \textquotedblleft{}neither food nor water\textquotedblright{}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ca · vā · kintu · na … na]{\sk{च} · \sk{वा} · \sk{किन्तु} · \sk{न} … \sk{न} — the four joins}

\label{lesson:SA-R52-joins}



\begin{quote}
Name the two joins that stand after the second item.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Before this chapter every Sanskrit sentence you could build named exactly one thing. Four small words later you can name two, offer a choice between them, set one against the other, and refuse both.

None of the four changed anything else in the sentence. That is the point worth carrying: Sanskrit joins by \textbf{placing a particle}, not by rearranging what is already there. When you meet the longer joins later — the ones that link whole clauses rather than nouns — they will behave the same way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{annaṁ pānīyaṁ ca}, then \emph{annaṁ pānīyaṁ vā}, and say what changed
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pānīyaṁ kṣīraṁ vā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{na annaṁ na pānīyam}
  \item \emph{Recall:} which of the four stands FIRST in its clause
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say all four joins in order, and for each one say where it stands.
\end{tcolorbox}
